note: The first De Franceschi families this archive has been able to document in Carnia itself — the country the family says it came from, and where every account of its origin has until now been tradition rather than record.

mione.claim: In 1679 a list of village headmen recorded, at Mione: «Zuane De Franceschi con un suo fiolo, Zuane d'Erman: questi tre nell'Istria, luogo imperiale» — a De Franceschi of Mione with a son, working in Istria, in the imperial place. Carlo De Franceschi, writing about 1873, said the family had come from Carnia and settled in Istria «intorno al 1700», and that De Franceschi were still living at Mione and Muina in his own day.
mione.found: They still were in 1939. Monsignor Lucio Soravito de Franceschi was born at Mione di Ovaro on 8 December 1939, ordained priest in 1963, professor of pastoral theology at the Udine seminary from 1977 and at the Faculty of Theology of Northern Italy from 1991, archpriest of Udine cathedral from 1999, and Bishop of Adria-Rovigo from 2004 to 2015. He died on 6 July 2019.
mione.why: Soravito is a Carnian house-name — soravìt, «above Vito's» — of the kind that fuses onto a surname to tell one branch of a village family from another. A Soravito de Franceschi at Mione is a De Franceschi of Mione with the house attached. Two hundred and sixty years after the headmen's list, the name is still in the village.

registers.what: The Archivio di Stato di Udine has digitised the Napoleonic civil registers of the Comune di Mione — fifty-nine volumes of births, marriages, deaths, marriage banns and marriage allegati, 1806 onward — and publishes them openly on the Antenati portal. Nobody had looked.
registers.index: The alphabetical index of births for 1806–1810 opens on three De Franceschi entries, the first three lines of the whole book: Anna-Maria, Anna-Cecilia and Gio: Batta. A few lines below are four Erman entries — the other family named in the 1679 headmen's list, still in the same village a hundred and thirty years later.

registers.read: Three things follow. First, the family is simply there, in the village, in the ordinary registers — not merely listed as working abroad. Second, one of them is a TAILOR, which is exactly the trade of the cramars who walked the road of the Furlans into Istria from the sixteenth century; another is a carpenter and the rest are farmers, which is the ordinary spread of a mountain commune. And third, the name they gave a son born at Mione on 15 October 1810 was GIOVANNI BATTISTA — the name of the man Carlo De Franceschi said built the family's house at Gologorica in 1711, and the name of the farmer of house 5 at Gračišće born in 1787.

paluzza.what: The earliest of them. Zuanne is the Venetian form of Giovanni — the same name the 1679 list gives the man of Mione.

muina.heading: The house at Muina, four generations deep
muina.intro: The marriage register goes further than the births. Napoleonic marriage acts read the couple's birth certificates into the record, and birth certificates name the grandparents. One act at Mione therefore reaches further back into Carnia than anything else this project has found.

chain.what: Dead before 1808. Named only as «qm. Leonardo» — the late Leonardo — in his son's style. If his grandson was born in 1788 and his son was of age to marry by about 1785, Leonardo belongs to a generation born somewhere between about 1710 and 1740.

chain.who: Antonio de Franceschi, son of the late Leonardo, and Maria née Corva
chain.what:
Farmers of Muina. **Antonio was dead before the wedding.** His written consent is dated **25 October 1807**, but by **28 January 1808** the notary styles his son *«Osvaldo del fu Antonio de Franceschi»* and takes a second, separate consent from **«Donna Maria nata Corva, vedova del fu Antonio de Franceschi»** — the widow. Under the Napoleonic Code the mother's consent was required only when the father was dead, so the second act is the procedural proof of the first fact.

Between those two documents lies a death nobody recorded here: **Antonio died between 25 October 1807 and 28 January 1808**, a window of fourteen weeks. Maria could not write; the notary noted it.

chain.who: Osvaldo de Franceschi and Appolonia Galante
chain.what: He was born at Muina on **14 March 1788** — the date given twice, by the marriage act and, independently, by the parish priest's certified extract of 21 January 1808 — and was twenty when he married on 28 January 1808; a farmer, and he signs his own name. His full baptismal name was **Osvaldo Antonio**, for the father who would be dead before he married. She was born at Muina on 3 May 1782, daughter of Antonio, son of the late Pietro Galante, and Speranza née Micoli.
Born at Muina at eleven in the morning on 30 December 1809, and presented to the registrar by the midwife Speranza Galante — who was, by the marriage act, her own maternal grandmother.

muina.leonardo: One name in that chain is worth stopping on. Carlo De Franceschi, writing to Kobler about 1873, said the house at Gologorica was built in 1711 by his trisavolo «Giambattista del fu Leonardo» — Giovanni Battista, son of the late Leonardo. And here, in the Carnian village Carlo said the family came from, is an «Antonio qm. Leonardo de Franceschi». The generations do not line up for the two Leonardos to be the same man: Carlo's Leonardo was the father of someone building a house in 1711, while this one is the grandfather of a boy born in 1788, three generations later. What it shows is that Leonardo was a name this family used, in this village — and that is the first time any name from Carlo's account of his own ancestry has turned up in a Carnian De Franceschi household in a register.
muina.witnesses: The four witnesses were Angelo Micoli, fifty-seven; Floriano Micoli, forty; Giuseppe Varnier, forty-eight; and Odorico Micoli, twenty-three — all farmers of Muina. The registrar was Valentino Lupieri. Micoli, Lupieri, Gortan, Brencis, Galante, Corva, Varnier: the same dozen surnames run through every document in this village.

allegati.heading: The papers behind the wedding
allegati.lead: The marriage act is a summary. **The allegati are the documents it summarises** — the loose sheets the couple actually carried to the registrar, bound afterwards into the year's file and digitised by the Archivio di Stato di Udine as *Mione, Matrimoni allegati, 1808*. Five of its seventy-eight pages are this marriage, and they say things the register does not.
rows: The father's consent is missing, and that is the point

The register recites a paternal consent of **25 October 1807**. The file does not contain it. What it contains instead is a **maternal** consent, taken on 28 January 1808 by the notary **Giacomo Micoli del fu Francesco** in his study at Muina, from **«Donna Maria nata Corva, vedova del fu Antonio de Franceschi»**, *«ad istanza fattale da suo figlio Osvaldo»* — at the request of her son. A widow's consent is what the Code required when the father had died. **Antonio was alive in October and dead in January.**
The bride's father consents separately

The same notary, the same day, takes the consent of **Antonio Galante del fu Pietro** of Muina for his daughter **Appolonia**. Both acts carry the same two witnesses — **Angelo Micoli** and **Zuane Fabris**, farmers of Muina.
Two baptismal extracts, written out by the priest

Both are certified at **Luincis on 21 January 1808** by **D. Giovanni Battista Dazio**, parish priest of the **Pieve Matrice di Gorto**, and authenticated at Mione on 28 January by the civil officer **Valentino Lupieri**. The groom's reads *«Osvaldo — Antonio figlio legittimo e naturale di Antonio quondam Leonardo Deffranceschi e di Maria sua moglie di Muina, egli è venuto alla luce li 14 del mese di Marzo dell'anno 1788, come rilevo dal Libro dei Battezzati»*. The bride's gives **Appolonia, daughter of Antonio quondam Pietro Galante, born 3 May 1782**.

That is the register's own dates confirmed from a second hand — and it names the book they came out of. **The baptisms of this family are in the Pieve di Gorto, in the Luincis section.** The Pieve is the mother church of the whole Val di Gorto, and it is the next thing to ask for.
Galante, and the priest who wrote it Salante

The notary writes the bride's surname **Galante**, in a clear looped G, in **both** of his acts. The parish priest, in the baptismal extract, writes **Salante** with a plain S; so does the clerk who docketed the file *«De Franceschi Osvaldo / Salante Appolonia»*.

**The marriage register settles it: Galante.** The act of 28 January 1808 gives *«Appolonia Galante … figlia di Antonio Galante e di Speranza nata Micoli»* — twice, in the same looped G as the notary's. Add **Pietro Galante**, who signed his own name at Mione in 1813 in a plain lower-case g, and the count is four independent hands for Galante against two for Salante — **one of them the man's own signature**.

**This archive had it the other way round for months**, and corrected it on 14 September 2026. The priest's *Salante* is kept on the record as what he actually wrote, because he was copying from the baptismal book and that is where the variant lives.
Who could write

**Neither parent could sign.** The notary records that Maria Corva *«non sa scrivere»* and that Galante likewise could not. Their children both signed the marriage act in their own hands. **The literacy arrives in one generation**, and these five sheets are where it can be watched happening.
allegati.close: None of this was found by searching. It was found by **paging past the first page of a search result** — the file had been counted as read on the strength of a listing that showed ten rows of a set that has twenty-six.

households1806.heading: Five De Franceschi households at Mione and Muina, 1806–1810
households1806.intro: Put every act together and the village stops being a name in a tradition and becomes a set of families with trades, wives, in-laws and children. All of it inside five years of one small commune's registers.

rows.who: Osvaldo de Franceschi († before 1806) and Catterina née Fabris
rows.evidence: Named in their daughter's marriage act of 7 August 1806. Giacoma, born 25 May 1789, seventeen years two months and twelve days old, married Ignazio di Prato, a merchant of Chialina. She signs herself «Giacoma de Franceschi q.m Osualdo». Her father had given written consent on 7 September 1805, so he died between then and the wedding.

rows.who: Antonio de Franceschi, son of the late Leonardo, and Maria née Corva
rows.evidence: Named in their son's marriage act of 28 January 1808, with Antonio's written consent of 25 October 1807. Leonardo, Antonio's father, was already dead — and so, by the wedding day, was Antonio: the allegati of that marriage take the consent from his widow.

rows.who: Osvaldo de Franceschi (b. 14 March 1788) and Appolonia Galante (b. 3 May 1782)
rows.evidence: Married 28 January 1808. Daughter Anna Maria born 30 December 1809, presented by the midwife Speranza Galante — Appolonia's own mother.

rows.who: Osvaldo de Franceschi and Valentina, or Cattarina, née Prencis
rows.evidence: Married 6 August 1807 (marriage index). Son Giovanni Battista born 15 October 1810, where the mother is written Cattarina nata Brencis — probably the same woman under a second baptismal name.

rows.who: Francesco de' Franceschi (b. about 1784) and Margherita née Gortan
rows.evidence: Daughter Anna Cecilia born 14 January 1810. He signs the register himself.

rows.who: Pasqua de' Franceschi, wife of Pietro Luchin
rows.evidence: Named as the mother in act 2 of 1810.

households1806.tailors: Look at who witnessed Giacoma's wedding in 1806: Gio: Battà Prencis, thirty-six, tailor; Gio: Battà del Missier, fifty-four, tailor; Giuseppe Pol, thirty-four, tailor; Pietro Rupil of Ovasta, thirty-six, tailor. Four tailors standing up at a merchant's wedding in an alpine village of a few hundred people. That is the cramar economy in a single line — the needle trades of the Canale di Gorto that sent men down the road of the Furlans into Istria every autumn from the sixteenth century. Francesco de' Franceschi of Mione was one of them in 1810.
households1806.micoli: And the registrar in 1806 is Giovanni Micoli-Toscano, with Battà Micoli-Toscano as secretary. The Micoli Toscano family archive at Mione is already on this project's research log as the place that holds the Gorto contracts naming the Erman who travelled to Istria with Zuane De Franceschi in 1679. In 1806 they are running the commune.

deaths.heading: And eight deaths in the same five years
deaths.intro: The register of the dead for the Comune di Mione, 1806–1810, carries eight De Franceschi entries. Read with the births, they turn a set of names into a family that was living and dying in one village.

rows.name: Leonarda Defranceschi
rows.note: Leonarda is the feminine of Leonardo — the name that stands at the head of the Muina chain.

rows.name: Anna Cecilia Defranceschi
rows.note: Born 14 January 1810 to Francesco the tailor and Margherita Gortan. She lived eleven days.

rows.name: Sebastiano Defranceschi, chierico
rows.note: A cleric — chierico, a man in minor orders. The only one of the name in these registers.

deaths.read: Two of these change what was already written on this page. Anna Cecilia, whose birth act was quoted above as evidence that a De Franceschi tailor lived at Mione in 1810, died eleven days after she was born; her father had carried her to the town hall at three in the morning and was back within a fortnight. And there is a Leonarda in 1808 and a Sebastiano in minor orders in 1810 — a family big enough to put a son into the church and to keep reusing its own names. The same index also records Corva and Erman deaths: Osvaldo Corva of Agrons in 1807, Teresa Corva of Muina the same year, and three Erman.

deepest.heading: The allegati, and the deepest name of all
deepest.intro: Napoleonic marriage files carry allegati — the supporting papers. Giacoma's file at Mione holds two, and one of them is a parish certificate written out by hand, sealed, and stamped with a two-and-sixpence revenue stamp of the Kingdom of Italy.
deepest.quote: Certifico io sottoscritto Parroco della Pieve Matrice di Gorto a parte Luvincis, come Giacoma figlia legitima e naturale di Osualdo quondam Gio: Batta de' Franceschi di Mione, e di Cattarina sua moglie, essa è nata li 25 del mese di Maggio nell'anno 1789, come consta dal Libro dei Battezzi.
deepest.trans: I, the undersigned parish priest of the mother church of Gorto at Luincis, certify that Giacoma, lawful and natural daughter of Osvaldo, son of the late GIOVANNI BATTISTA de' Franceschi of Mione, and of Cattarina his wife, was born on the 25th of May in the year 1789, as appears from the Book of Baptisms.
deepest.why: That pushes the Mione family back one more generation, to a GIOVANNI BATTISTA DE' FRANCESCHI who was already dead by 1789. And it means that both of the names Carlo De Franceschi gave for his own ancestors — Giambattista, and the Leonardo who was Giambattista's father — occur in the eighteenth-century De Franceschi of Mione: a Giovanni Battista dead before 1789, and an Antonio son of the late Leonardo. Carlo said the family came from Carnia. In the village he named, the two names he used are the two names in the register.
deepest.care: This is still not a descent. Giovanni Battista and Leonardo were among the commonest names in Friuli, the generations do not align, and no document yet connects any Mione household to any Istrian one. What has changed is that the claim now has a place, a parish, a set of households and two matching names — instead of a single line in a list of headmen.
deepest.next: The certificate also names the record that would settle it: the LIBRO DEI BATTEZZI of the Pieve Matrice di Gorto at Luincis, which in 1806 still held baptisms back beyond 1789. That book, and the parish's marriage and death books, are the next thing to ask for — from the parish itself or from the Archivio Storico Diocesano at Udine. Ask for De Franceschi at Mione and Muina between 1650 and 1800.

ginut.heading: The dal Ginut household at Mione
ginut.lead: Until now the Carnia page could show that the surname existed at Mione — in a headmen's list of 1679, in the Napoleonic registers of 1806–10, in a bishop born there in 1939 — but not a single household in the round. Two Geneanet pages held in the family's own files give one: five generations of De Franceschi at Mione, with their trades, their house-names and their Friulian, published by a member who signs himself «carnia».
ginut.why: It matters for three reasons. The house-name «dal Ginut» is how a Carnian village actually identifies a family, and this archive has never had one for a De Franceschi. The trade of the head of the house in the nineteenth century is «tessitore contadino» — peasant weaver — which is precisely the trade Carlo De Franceschi's own book says sent the men of the Ovaro parishes down the road of the Furlans into Istria as cramars. And in the wife's ancestry stands the surname ERMAN — the family named alongside Zuane De Franceschi in the 1679 list of men working in the imperial part of Istria.

chain.what: Dates unrecorded. The by-name of the house Francesco was born in — «in cjasa da Prences» — is hers.

Born at Mione 16 June 1816, died there in August 1906 — ninety years in one village. His wife, born at Mione 20 November 1820, died on 3 December 1852, four months after bearing the son below. Her own line runs back through Giovanni Battista Giorgis (1781–1828) and Giovanni Pietro Giorgis (1749–1828) to Maddalena ERMAN, daughter of Benedetto Erman.

chain.who: Francesco Arcangelo De Franceschi, called Checo dal Ginut
chain.what: Born at Mione 5 August 1852 «in cjasa da Prences»; died at Mione 9 June 1939 «in cjasa dal Ginut». Trade: tessitore contadino — tiessitôr contadin, a peasant weaver. Married 23 April 1887 Maria Giuseppina Fedele of Clavais, born 3 February 1856, died at Mione 25 February 1934.

chain.who: Leopoldo Eugenio De Franceschi, called Poldo dal Ginut
chain.what: Born at Mione 15 September 1900 «dal Ginut». Trade: marangon boscador — carpenter and woodsman. Married 4 March 1931 in the church of St Peter at Givigliana, Giacomina Gortana, born there 20 October 1912, died at Tolmezzo 7 September 1983. He died at Udine 30 September 1973 and was buried at Ovaro the next day, «alla Pieve di Gorto». Two photographs of him survive, of 1920 and 1939.

children.heading: The seven children of Checo and Maria, 1888–1900

rows.what: Died four days after the war in Europe ended.
Ninety-four years, born and died in the same village.

notes.heading: What the family says about itself, in Friulian
notes.lead: The Geneanet notes are not in Italian. They are in Carnian Friulian, written by somebody who had the story from the people in it, and they explain how a weaver came to hold the house he died in.

rows.fur: Checo al va a sta in cuc dal Ginut, dula ca steva Maria in cjasa di URBAN Leopoldo e la so femina CLEVA (so agna?) e il fradi di Leopoldo, Eugenio.
rows.en: Checo went to live up at the Ginut, where Maria was living, in the house of Urban Leopoldo and his wife Cleva — her aunt? — and Leopoldo's brother Eugenio.

rows.fur: Dal Ginut a era l'ostaria butada ju dal 1900, no vin frutz a lasin la roba a Checo e Maria.
rows.en: At the Ginut there was the inn, pulled down in 1900. They had no children, so they left the property to Checo and Maria.

rows.fur: Maridâs ta glesio di St Pieari a Gjviano e las a sta i Mion dal GINUT, in cjasa di Checo e Maria.
rows.en: Married in the church of St Peter at Givigliana, and went to live at Mione at the Ginut, in the house of Checo and Maria.

rows.fur: Nascût a Mion in cjasa da Prences … A Mion in cjasa dal Ginut.
rows.en: Born at Mione in the Prences house … [died] at Mione in the Ginut house. The two ends of one life, each fixed by the name of a house rather than a street or a number.

ginut.close: No descent is claimed and none is available. This household cannot be joined to the Istrian line, and nothing here says it should be. What it does is turn the Carnia argument from a list of stray entries into a family that can be looked at: weavers and woodsmen at Mione for five generations, holding a house they inherited from an innkeeper who had no children, marrying Fedele of Clavais and Gortana of Givigliana and carrying Erman blood — the same surname that stands beside a De Franceschi of Mione in the one document that shows the movement into Istria at all.
ginut.ask: The Geneanet member who published this signs himself «carnia» and has clearly worked the Ovaro registers directly. He is the single most useful contact this archive has identified: he can say whether GioBatta's line goes back past Paolo, and whether any De Franceschi of Mione left for Istria.

second_document.heading: A second document, found in 2026
second_document.text: This page has said since it was written that the headmen's list of 1679 is the only document showing the movement from Carnia into Istria at all. That is no longer true. Giovanni Kobler, going through the civic records of Fiume in the 1870s, wrote out for Carlo De Franceschi the Defranceschi households of that city — and his second entry reads: «Valentino Defranceschi, venuto dalla Carnia, fu fatto Cittadino nel 1739.» Come from Carnia; made a citizen in 1739. With his wife Elena he had ten sons and four daughters, a house in the Capuchins' quarter and a vineyard at Plase; in 1764 he built the Chapel of St Helen; he made himself a tomb in the cathedral with an epigraph in 1785, and died that year.
second_document.why: It connects nobody to this family — Carlo himself first thought the Fiume harbour-master descended from this Valentino, and then withdrew it. What it does is turn the mechanism from tradition into record. Carnians of this surname demonstrably came down into the Kvarner in the eighteenth century, and one of them left a chapel and a tomb that can still be looked for.
second_document.source: Jakov Jelinčić's edition of Kobler's letters, Vjesnik historijskih arhiva u Rijeci i Pazinu, open access on Hrčak.

weavers.heading: What the 1679 list was a list of
weavers.lead: This archive has leaned on one line from a headmen's return of 1679 — a Zuane De Franceschi of Mione, at work in the Habsburg County of Pazin — and has been arguing from it that the family came down into Istria as weavers. Giorgio Ferigo, the historian of the Carnian population, quotes that return in full in «Le cifre, le anime», and the argument turns out not to need making. The list is a list of weavers. It says so.
weavers.quote: …nell'elenco stilato dai merighi, compaiono soltanto i tessitori recatisi nella contea di Pisino: così da Agrons e Cella «Mathio Ruvis con doi fioli, Gio-Batta et Pietro da Ruvis: questi tre nell'Istria, luogo imperiale»; da Mione «Zuane De Franceschi con un suo fiolo, Zuane d'Erman: questi tre nell'Istria, luogo imperiale»; da Luint «Anzolo del Fabro, mogliato nell'Istria, luogo imperiale».
weavers.en: …in the list drawn up by the headmen there appear only the weavers who had gone into the County of Pisino: so from Agrons and Cella, «Mathio Ruvis with two sons, Gio-Batta and Pietro da Ruvis: these three in Istria, imperial territory»; from Mione, «Zuane De Franceschi with a son of his, Zuane d'Erman: these three in Istria, imperial territory»; from Luint, «Anzolo del Fabro, married in Istria, imperial territory».

gains.lab: The trade is stated, not inferred
gains.text: «soltanto i tessitori» — only the weavers. The return was made to a question about the County of Pisino, and the men enumerated in it are tessitori. Everything this archive had built as a convergence — the peasant weaver at the head of the Mione household, Leonardo De Franceschi the one trained weaver at Gologorica — now sits on top of a source that says the word.

gains.lab: Zuane had a son with him
gains.text: «con un suo fiolo» — with a son of his. The line this archive has been quoting for months names two Defranceschi in Istria in 1679, not one, travelling together with a third man, Zuane d'Erman. Three from Mione.

gains.lab: And the numbers are an undercount
gains.text: Ferigo is explicit that the return covers only the imperial county, because that is all the question asked about. Venetian Istria — where, he says, the great majority of these villages' men documentably went — is simply not in the answer. Whatever the 1679 list shows of Carnian weavers in Istria is a floor, not a ceiling.

road.heading: The road they took, and how old it was

rows.lab: January 1511
rows.text: One Michele del Canal di Gorto — «più che probabilmente di Ovaro» — buys a «partem botege textorie», a share in a weaver's shop, at Montona in Istria. The deed is in the protocols of the notaries Daniele and Nicolò de Vidonis of Cella, in the Biblioteca Civica of Udine. It is the earliest of the line.

rows.lab: 10 October 1540
rows.text: Jacobo Carlavariis of Luincis dictates his will at Pedena in Istria. Pedena is the cathedral town of the diocese this family's own two parishes belonged to. A Carnian weaver from the next village to Mione was dying there a hundred and forty years before the 1679 list.

Further back and further south, a «Petrus de Cargna, magister textor qm. magistri Christophori» is living at Sissano near Pola. Ferigo notes honestly that it is not known whether he came from the lower Gorto or was an isolated case.

rows.lab: The road itself
rows.text: «la strada dei furlani» — the Friulians' road, running from the parishes of Ovaro and Luincis into Istria. Ferigo's summary of the documents: relatively rare in the sixteenth century, thick in the seventeenth, thickest in the eighteenth. The family's own crossing, somewhere around 1700, sits in the thickest part of it.

road.where: And the destinations were specific. «i Timeus, i Misdariis, i Zanus, i Lupieri, i Micoli, gli Spinotti, i Dell'Oste, i Candriella da Ovasta, Luint, Mione, Cella, Muina, Cludinico si portano a Verteneglio, Sissano, Buje, Città Nova, San Pietro in Selve a esercitare la tessitura» — named families from named villages, Mione among them, going to named places in Istria to weave. They bought or built a house and a smallholding or a vineyard, and sent oil and the sharp wine of the Karst back up to the people who had stayed.
road.word: One sentence of Ferigo's is worth the whole section: «onde dire cargnel in Istria equivaleva a dire tessitore» — so that to say cargnel, Carnian, in Istria was the same as saying weaver. That is what the family would have been called when it arrived.

weavers.lawsuit: A footnote to the trade, because it says what kind of men these were. For fifty years between the late seventeenth century and the mid-eighteenth the linen-merchants of Udine fought the Carnian weavers in the courts. The merchants' complaint: the weavers, «cui è saltato un verme nella testa di voler a pretesto di devozione erigere una scuola» — in whose heads a worm has jumped, wanting to erect a guild under pretext of devotion — are not content with the profit they already draw from the freedom to practise the craft in the city, and take everything home «dove soggiornano per lo più le loro famiglie ed essi si trasferiscono più mesi all'anno», where their families mostly live and to which they themselves return for several months of the year. Seasonal men with families in the mountains, organising, and being resented for it.

notary.heading: And a place to look next, with a shelfmark
notary.text: The inventory of Ovaro sources in the Archivio di Stato di Udine, printed in «Ovaro: itinerari e ricerche» (1995), lists the old notarial archive by notarial seat. Under «Sede notarile: Mione» stands: «B. 2979 Franceschi Gio. Batta — 2 protocolli istrumenti 1737–1783, 1 minutario 1757–1783». A notary of the family's own surname held the seat at Mione for forty-six years, and his deeds survive. Two boxes further on: «B. 2985 Soravito Franceschi Antonio — 2 protocolli istrumenti e testamenti 1800–1805».
notary.why: Every contract and will drawn at Mione between 1737 and 1783 passed through the hands of a Giovanni Battista Franceschi and is in one box in Udine. That period covers exactly the years in which a Valentino Defranceschi «venuto dalla Carnia» was made a citizen of Fiume — 1739 — and the generations Carlo says came over. It is the most specific unopened door this archive has on the Carnian side, and it needs a letter, not a search box.

weavers.sourcing: Giorgio Ferigo, «Le cifre, le anime. Scritti di storia della popolazione e della mobilità in Carnia» (Udine, 2010) — read from the copy at the Internet Archive, September 2026; the 1679 passage is at page 100, in the chapter «Le stagioni dei migranti». «Ovaro: itinerari e ricerche» (Quaderni del Centro regionale di Catalogazione e Restauro, 1995), the section «Fonti ovaresi nell'Archivio di Stato di Udine» by Luana Pasut, likewise. Both are free.

brhan.heading: There is a whole scholarly literature on this migration, and the family is in it
brhan.lead: Dorotea Brhan, «Emigrazione dalla Carnia verso l'Istria (XVI–XIX sec.)», in the «Atti» of Rovigno, volume 34 of 2004, pages 473–494. Twenty-two pages on precisely the movement this family made, built from the parish and notarial books in the state archive at Pazin. Until this week the archive was arguing the Carnian crossing from one line of a headmen's list. It turns out to be a documented phenomenon with its own name, its own sociology and its own bibliography.

rows.lab: What they were called and what they did
rows.text: Cargnelli — the Carnian mountain men — «da secoli costretti a spostarsi, almeno stagionalmente, in cerca di migliori condizioni di vita», forced for centuries to move, at least seasonally, north into the German lands, south to Istria and the upper Adriatic, west into the Veneto. Some were cramars, pedlars with their crassigne packs, crossing Istria in every direction. Others «erano semplicemente tesseri, tessitori a domicilio» — were simply weavers, weaving at home. Quirino Ermacora's line on them: «emigrano d'inverno e travagliano giorno e notte per procacciarsi con la fatica e coll'industria sussidi per la loro vecchiaia» — they go out in winter and work night and day to earn, by toil and industry, a provision for their old age.

rows.lab: They were a third thing in the village
rows.text: Tommasini, writing in the seventeenth century of Sanvincenti: «tra essi si trovano molte famiglie di cargnelli, ch'attendono alla mercantia et alcune poche persone civili che vestono all'Italiana» — among them are many families of cargnelli, who attend to trade, and a few civil persons who dress in the Italian way. Brhan draws the conclusion: the Cargnelli were seen as a group apart from both the Croats of the countryside and the Italians of the castle, bilingual because their business made them so. That is the position a family arriving from Mione would have occupied.

rows.lab: And then they bought land and became Dominus
rows.text: «Nel Settecento molti Cargnelli investivano i soldi guadagnati con l'industria comprando beni immobili dalle popolazioni locali» — in the eighteenth century many of them put the money they had earned by their trade into property bought from the local people, most often vineyards, the most profitable crop inland. «Nelle fonti vengono indicati con l'indicazione D.no, domino, ovvero proprietario terriero, chiaro segno di una stratificazione sociale già in atto non riscontrabile nei secoli precedenti» — in the sources they are then marked D.no, domino, landowner: a clear sign of a social stratification now under way that the earlier centuries do not show.

rows.lab: Among them, a De Franceschi
rows.text: «Gran parte dei Carnici di Sanvincenti, nella seconda metà del XVIII secolo, risulta tra i proprietari terrieri come ad esempio D.no Vittorio De Franceschi, D.no Valentin Lupieri, D.no Antonio Fabris.» A Dominus Vittorio De Franceschi at Sanvincenti in the later eighteenth century, listed among the Carnian landholders — beside a Lupieri, which is the name of the notary who held the seat at Luint, the next village to Mione, from 1699 to 1724. The purchases are in the protocols of the Sanvincenti notary Alvise Davia, 1787–1789, in the state archive at Pazin.

rows.lab: Another Mione family, and where it ended up
rows.text: Brhan compares the eighteenth-century archives with Roberto Starec's survey of 1945 and finds the descendants still in place: «i discendenti di Gio. Batta Giorgis di Mione vivevano ancora a San Pietro in Selve, quelli di Pietro Antonio Rodella di Ovaro a Torre e quelli di Gio. Batta Candriella di Claudinico a Visignano». A second family out of Mione — the Giorgis, who also appear in the Mione papers in the Udine archive — still at San Pietro in Selve in 1945, which is twenty kilometres from Gologorica.

rows.lab: They rose
rows.text: Carnians became zuppani, village headmen: Gio. Batta Rabas at Visignano in 1768, from a family three generations in the place; Giacomo Cadore in 1750 and 1769; Francesco Dell'Osto as early as 1678. And the mistri got the good commissions — Gio. Maria Rabassi «de Cargna, perito nell'arte di muraro» built the marble altar of St Quirinus in the parish church at Visignano in 1736.

brhan.why: Set this beside the Gologorica registers and the shape of the family's first century in Istria stops being mysterious. A «Dominus Josephus Defranceschi» stands godparent there through the 1760s and 1770s; a «Sig.r Piero De Franceschi da Gollogorizza» marries a noble Bembo at Valle in 1795. Brhan's article says exactly what that title meant for a Carnian family in Istria in that decade: not old standing, but a weaver's or pedlar's earnings turned into a vineyard, and the notary writing D.no in front of the name for the first time. The family did not arrive as gentry. It bought its way to the word.
brhan.source: Dorotea Brhan, «Emigrazione dalla Carnia verso l'Istria (XVI–XIX sec.)», Atti del Centro di ricerche storiche di Rovigno, vol. XXXIV (2004), pp. 473–494 — read from the copy at the Internet Archive, September 2026. Her sources are the parish and notarial books in the Državni arhiv u Pazinu, which is also where this archive's own Gologorica registers are.

gorto.heading: Santa Maria di Gorto: the other end of the road
gorto.lead: Everything on this page until now has been read at a distance — a headmen's list of 1679 quoted in a book, a notary's box number in an inventory, a surname in an index. Then the family drove up the Val Degano and walked into the graveyard at the Pieve di Santa Maria di Gorto, above Ovaro, and photographed what was on the stones. There are more De Franceschi in that one cemetery than this archive has found in the whole of Istria.

churches.lab: The Pieve di Santa Maria di Gorto
churches.text: At Luincis above Ovaro: the mother church of the whole Val di Gorto, to which Mione, Muina, Agrons, Cella, Ovasta, Luint and the rest were subject, and the churchyard the valley's dead go to. The provincial panel at its door: «una delle undici antiche pievi della Carnia, risale probabilmente al secolo VIII» — one of the eleven ancient pievi of Carnia, probably eighth-century. It burned, and in 1431 was rebuilt by «maestro Stefano quondam Simone di Mena»; the present building is eighteenth-century and keeps fragments of what came before. Three naves, four arcades a side on three piers, a square apse facing east. In the apse survive Romanesque fresco fragments of the Parable of the Wise and Foolish Virgins, the figures set inside a thin painted architecture of twisted columns and finely decorated arches. The organ is of 1778, by Giovanni Battista de Corte of Ovasta — in Friulian, Zuan Batiste de Cort de Davaste. There is a small museum inside. If any one place on earth is the origin of this line, on the evidence assembled here, it is the parish that buries in this ground.

churches.lab: The Chiesa di Sant'Antonio at Mione
churches.text: The village church itself, and the provincial sign at its door dates it to the fifteenth century. The apse carries what the sign calls the finest fresco cycle by the painter Pietro Fuluto, painted about 1510 — the Annunciation, God the Father and the Evangelists in the vault; on the walls the Nativity, the Presentation, the Flight into Egypt, the Slaughter of the Innocents and the Resurrection; Apostles in the lower band of the apse. The influence of Gianfrancesco da Tolmezzo is noted as remarkable. On the counter-façade stands a wooden ancona of 1538 by Simone di Paolo of Udine: three tiers, with St Maurice, St Anthony and St Bovo below, St Vincent, the Madonna and Child and St Florian in the middle, and Christ Resurrected above between painted panels of the Madonna and the Angel of the Annunciation.

churches.lab: And this archive has met that painter already
churches.text: «Ovaro: itinerari e ricerche», the 1995 survey read here in September, records the same man as «Pietro Fuluto (Mione, ante 1514; Liariis 1515 e Luincis 1519)» — frescoing Mione before 1514, Liariis in 1515, Luincis in 1519. The cycle in the family's own village church is the earliest of the three. A Zuane De Franceschi walking out of Mione for Istria in 1679 had grown up under those walls.

stones: Agostino De Franceschi
b. 2[2 or 8] July 18[??], d. 1[1 or 5] September 18[??]

The oldest De Franceschi stone in the ground, and the archive has now failed twice to read it. The inscription was cut, then effaced when the stone was reused, and FRANCESCO DE FRANCESCHI 1887–1945 and LIDUINA CECCONI 1897–1977 were applied over it in metal letters. What is certain: «Qui giace / AGOSTINO DE FRANCESCHI / Nato 2? Luglio 18?? / Morto 1? Settembre 18?? / Moglie e [figli] / posero». A man buried by his wife and children, and the months July and September. Two readings of the same photographs have given 26 July 1822 and 22 July 1853 for the birth, 11 September and 15 September for the death. Enlarged, the birth day is a 2 followed by a 2 or an 8; the death day a 1 followed by a 1 or a 5; and the years are inside a blown highlight that no amount of processing recovers — pushed hard, the stone's own crystal texture starts producing digits that are not there. This entry now says what the stone says and no more. It wants one photograph in raking light, and the Ovaro civil death register would settle it outright.
Antonio De Franceschi
With MARTA ANZOLA 1875–1964, «figli e figlie». An oval photograph of the couple is set into the stone.
Gio: Batta De Franceschi
With TERESA COMUZZI 1886–1963, «i figli». Husband and wife died in the same year; two portraits flank a carved Madonna and Child.
Umberto De Franceschi
With CORVA MARIANNA 1896–1979. He lived to ninety-six.
Sebastiano Soravito De Franceschi
With MARIA ROIA in SORAVITO DE FRANCESCHI 1856–1930, «i figli dolenti posero», and GIACOMINA SORAVITO 1886–1967 added below.
Sebastiano Soravito De Franceschi
A second stone and a second man of the name, a generation later. With ANNA CROSILLA ved. SORAVITO DE FRANCESCHI, d. 1990.
Maddalena De Franceschi

Twice: on her own worn stone with LUIGI GIORGIS 1875–1950, «i figli dolenti posero», and again on the later FAM. GIORGIS monument with Lodovico, Serafino, Caterina Micoli, Annamaria Giorgis 1933–1997 and Lucia Garettini 1933–2023.
Amalia De Franceschi
On the ROVIS wall plaque, with FAUSTINO ROVIS 1874–1956; above them GIO. BATTA ROVIS 1841–1892 and CATERINA GIORGIS 1840–1919, and below ROVIS GUIDO 1907–1975. Three photographs.
Eufemia De Franceschi

With PUSTETTO FRANCESCO 1891–1978. On the same stone their sons AUGUSTO 1921–1943 and GIOBATTA 1922–1945, dead at twenty-two and twenty-three; CIMENTI PIETRO 1914–1990, photographed in clerical dress; and PUSTETTO MARIA MADDALENA 1926–2015, in a habit.
Aurelia De Franceschi
On the FAM. FELICE monument with GIUSEPPE FELICE 1900–1982, ELIO 1934–2017, ISIDORO FELICE 1940–2023 and DANTE FELICE 1933–2024.
Giulia De Franceschi
With ROBERTO PUCHER, on a marble tablet with a single oval photograph of the two of them, and the line «A RICORDO LA CUGINA NENA» — in memory, from cousin Nena.
Lice Adami De Franceschi
A twelfth stone, on polished granite with a framed photographic portrait: «DE FRANCESCHI — LICE ADAMI — 1914–2002». Adami is on the Muina war memorial too.
Isabella Dell'Oste, widow De Franceschi
dates not legible

A low kerbed grave, read at a distance and not yet square-on: «ISABELLA DELL'O[STE] — VED. DE FRA[NCESCHI]». Dell'Oste is one of the families Ferigo names as walking the road of the Furlans into Istria. If the reading holds it is a marriage between two of them.
Francesco De Franc[eschi]

A plaque with applied metal letters on a badly eroded older stone; the tail of the surname is behind a plant and the great stone behind it will not give up its lettering in flat light. It is very likely the Agostino stone of 1822 with a later addition. Wanted: raking light, early or late.
gorto.daughters: Count the eleven. Six of them are a De Franceschi woman under her husband's name — Felice, Giorgis, Rovis, Pucher, Pustetto, Soravito. At Mione the name survives as much through daughters marrying into the valley's other houses as through sons keeping it. That is what a small mountain parish looks like after three centuries of the same forty families.
gorto.neighbours: And look at who they are buried among. Giorgis. Micoli. Fabris. Timeus. Spinotti. Crosilla. Corva. Gardel. Beorchia. Menegon. Those are not random Friulian names. Giorgis is the family whose descendants Dorotea Brhan traced to San Pietro in Selve in Istria and still there in 1945, and whose house at San Pietro in Selve gave Kandler lunch in 1849. Fabris is a Dominus among the Carnian landowners of Sanvincenti. Timeus, Spinotti and Micoli are on Giorgio Ferigo's list of the families that walked the road of the Furlans into Istria. Crosilla is the name of a notary at Mione. Corva is the name in the 1808 Napoleonic act at Muina — «Antonio qm. Leonardo De Franceschi and Maria nata Corva». The people in the ground at Gorto are the same families as the people in the Istrian records. This graveyard is the other end of the road.
gorto.views: Two of the family's photographs are not of stones. One is taken from the air over Ovaro: the Degano running grey and braided down the valley floor, the lower village strung along the road, a hamlet high on the shoulder opposite with its own church tower, and the walled cemetery on its own terrace at the bottom right of the frame, apart from the houses. The other is the cemetery itself from the gate — wall-graves let into the enclosure on three sides, the standing stones in gravel between them, and behind and above it the octagonal stone campanile of the pieve with its conical spire and the white church beside it, with the cloud down on the ridges. The archive has had the name of this place for a year. It has not had the shape of it until now: a burial ground on a shelf of grass, walled, with the mother church of the valley standing over it.
gorto.furlani: And one that runs the other way. On a loculus plaque in the same cemetery: «INS. MARIO FURLANI — ALBONA 1912 — OVARO 1978» — a schoolteacher born at Albona in Istria in 1912 and buried at Ovaro in Carnia in 1978. Every argument on this page is about people going south from these valleys into Istria. Here is a man who came north, and died in the parish they left.

gorto_war.heading: And three war memorials with the name on them
gorto_war.lead: The valley put up its dead three times over, and a De Franceschi is on each.

rows.lab: Muina, inaugurated 22 August 1920
rows.text: «IN MEMORIA DEI CADUTI IN GUERRA», placed by «i compagni di Muina». Sixteen names of the First World War: Lieutenant Micoli Umberto, Corporal-Major Svander Giuseppe, Corporal Spinotti Giovanni, and then the privates — DE FRANCESCHI VITTORIO and DE FRANCESCHI ISIDORO, Stefani Aristide, Riccardo and Giacomo, Fabris Antonio, Micoli Riccardo, Beorchia Osvaldo, Menegon Leonardo, Lorenzini Giacomo and Michele, Corporal Stefani Antonio, Adami Giovanni.

rows.lab: Mione, on the road by the cemetery, set 19 September 1954
rows.text: «GUERRA 1940–1945», in two columns. Among the soldiers, two Spinotti dead and four DISPERSI — missing — the first of them DE FRANCESCHI ISIDORO, with Macuglia Donato, Menegon Aniceto and Micoli Sisto. And then the second column, headed «CIVILI CADUTI 1 E 2.XI.1944»: Stradiotto Angelina, DE FRANCESCHI EGIDIO, Fabris geom. Giovanni, Fabris Tullio, Felice Guido, Gallo Ettore, Micoli Elio.

rows.lab: And in the cemetery itself
rows.text: A second stone, «NOVEMBRE 1944 — MAGGIO 1945», carrying fourteen names with De Franceschi Egidio at the head of them, the same seven civilians of the first two days of November and seven more who died in the seven months that followed: Not Antonio, Not Lino, Not Secondo, Palma Eligio, Piemonte Paolino, Timeus Guerrino, Marin Antonio.

gorto_war.what: Seven civilians of one small village killed on the first and second of November 1944, and seven more before the war ended. Carnia in the autumn of 1944 had just had its partisan republic — the Repubblica libera della Carnia — and the German and Cossack sweep that put an end to it came through these valleys in exactly those days. This archive does not have the local account of what happened at Mione on 1 and 2 November and will not guess at it. What the two stones establish is the shape of it: a civilian killing, on a named date, in the village this family came from, with a De Franceschi among the dead.
gorto_war.isidoro: One name to keep straight. A DE FRANCESCHI ISIDORO is on the Muina memorial of 1920, dead in the First World War, and a DE FRANCESCHI ISIDORO is on the Mione memorial as missing in the Second. They cannot be the same man. The second was almost certainly named for the first — which is how these valleys carried their dead forward, and how a family archive gets caught if it is not careful.
gorto_war.todo: What the photographs cannot give: the ages, the parents and the house numbers. Those are in the Ovaro civil registers and in the Pieve's own books. But a name and two years on a stone is enough to order a certificate, and there are now eleven of them.

brhan2004.heading: «In partibus Carsi et Istriae» — the study that puts this family in its migration
brhan2004.lead: Dean Brhan's «L'emigrazione dalla Carnia verso l'Istria (XVI–XIX secolo)», in the Atti of Rovigno for 2004, is the study of the movement this whole page is about. It was read in full in September 2026, and it names this family twice — once in a sentence that states plainly what this archive has spent months trying to establish.

key.text: Listing the Istrian villages whose very names betray a Carnian root — Declevi, Cleva, Nadali, Danielisi, Cramari, Rovisi, Spinottia, Stanzia Lupieri, Lorenzini, Prenzi, Valenti — Brhan ends: «…e Grobenicco dei Carnelli, tra Moncalvo (luogo natio dei De Franceschi) e Valdarsa.» Grobenicco of the Carnians, between Moncalvo — the native place of the De Franceschi — and the Valdarsa. Moncalvo is Gologorica. In the standard study of the Carnian migration into Istria, this family's village is named as their «luogo natio» and they are counted among the immigrants without argument, as a thing everybody in that literature knows.

rows.lab: Why the movement left almost no records
rows.text: Brhan's argument is that this migration was continuous, long, individual and spontaneous — driven by economics, not organised by the state as the Morlach resettlements were. Because nobody organised it, nobody filed it. «The primary sources are therefore parish registers and local notarial acts, not government files.» That is exactly why this archive has spent its time in baptism books and notarial boxes rather than in state papers, and it is why the question has been so hard.

rows.lab: The phrase that gives the study its title
rows.text: A Venetian enquiry of 1769 recorded fifty-four Carnians in Istria — and the Carnian parish registers at the other end mark their absentees «in partibus Carsi et Istriae», in the parts of the Carso and Istria. The two ends of the road, each keeping half the record.

rows.lab: What they were, and what they did with the money
rows.text: They were craftsmen and traders — the «cramars» with their pedlar's crassigne — and they filled a total vacuum of artisan labour in a Slav-farming interior. They preferred the interior to the coast. They reinvested craft and trade profits in land bought from the local population; they kept property and kin in Carnia across generations; and they assimilated fast, often by the second generation, to whichever community was dominant locally. Weavers came especially from the Quartiere di Socchieve, and the majority of the Istrian Carnians from the Quartiere di Gorto and the Val Pesarina. Gorto is the pieve this page began at.

rows.lab: Kandler's own list, and a Stanza De Franceschi
rows.text: Brhan prints Pietro Kandler's mid-nineteenth-century list of the families of Carnian origin at Sanvincenti: «Lupieri, Fiorencis, Defranceschi, Fabris, Vernier, Gonano, Vorano, Zuliani, Crosilla, Sandri, Corva, Spinotti e altre». And among the farmsteads around the castle, most of them Carnian-owned, «Stanza Lupieri, Stanza Spinotto, Stanza De Franceschi». Antonio De Colle counted a hundred and eighteen surnames of Carnian-Friulian origin in the commune of Visignano alone, and Defranceschi is on that list too.

rows.lab: And four named eighteenth-century De Franceschi at Sanvincenti
rows.text: «D.no Vittorio De Franceschi» among the landed proprietors. And a marriage: Zuanne Volpe of Bergamasque origin married «Maria Zanco vedova di Gasparo De Franceschi, carnico pure lui» — widow of Gasparo De Franceschi, himself a Carnian — and came into his capital; her will leaves it, should their children die, to her first husband's kinswomen «Pasqua e Antonia De Franceschi». Four people, and an explicit statement that Gasparo was Carnian. Brhan takes this from an unpublished private study, so the archive records it as a lead needing the Pisino registers behind it — but a Carnian De Franceschi at Sanvincenti in the eighteenth century is a fact of the right shape.

rows.lab: A documented Mione line, though not of this surname
rows.text: «I discendenti di Gio. Batta Giorgis di Mione vivevano ancora a San Pietro in Selve, quelli di Pietro Antonio Rodella di Ovaro a Torre e quelli di Gio. Batta Candriella di Claudinico a Visignano.» The descendants of Gio. Batta Giorgis of Mione were still at San Pietro in Selve; those of Pietro Antonio Rodella of Ovaro at Torre. Named men from Mione and Ovaro, traced to named Istrian villages, still there in 1945. Not this surname — but Giorgis is on the Gorto stones this page transcribes, married to a Maddalena De Franceschi.

rows.lab: And Carlo, of Carnian descent, on the Carnians
rows.text: «Nell'Ottocento, in pieno clima nazionalistico e patriotico, Carlo De Franceschi si espresse criticamente sui Cargnelli di Lindaro perché “imbastarditisi sposando donne slave, giunsero a … parlare fra loro a preferenza lo slavo”.» In the nineteenth century, in a fully nationalist climate, Carlo De Franceschi spoke critically of the Carnians of Lindar because, having bastardised themselves by marrying Slav women, they came to speak Slav among themselves by preference. Carlo is the great-great-grandson of Carnian immigrants. He is describing the ordinary fate of families like his own, in the ugliest available word, because by 1860 it had become a political matter. It is the sharpest thing this archive has found about what he was, and it is not flattering.

brhan2004.source_brhan: Dean Brhan, «“In partibus Carsi et Istriae”: l'emigrazione dalla Carnia verso l'Istria (XVI–XIX secolo)», Atti del Centro di ricerche storiche di Rovigno XXXIV (2004), pp. 473–494, open access. Read in full September 2026 and held in this project's source library.

agrons.heading: Agrons — and the question this archive was built to ask is answered
agrons.lead: For months this site has said that the family came from Carnia and could not say from where. On 7 September 2026 three independent sources arrived within an hour of each other and gave the same answer, and the family had already driven to the place and photographed its graveyard without knowing that was what it was.

carlo.lab: First, Carlo himself, in a letter this archive already owned
carlo.q: Anche i miei derivano dalla Carnia, ma si stabilirono in Istria intorno al 1700. Il mio trisavolo fabbricò la nostra casa nel 1711 come da relativa iscrizione. … A quanto mi narrava il suddetto Corrado, per tradizioni o scritti conservati nella sua famiglia, i nostri in origine erano da Bergamo, poi venuti in Carnia, dove avevano castelli, poi fortemente decaduti si dispersero. Ma ve n'ha tuttodì a Mione e Muina della Carnia. Noi abbiamo stemma: nella parte superiore dello scudo una croce greca attraversata da due freccie, nell'inferiore un melagrano; sovra lo scudo elmo piumato.
carlo.en: Mine too come from Carnia, but they settled in Istria around 1700. My great-great-grandfather built our house in 1711, as the inscription on it says. … According to what the said Corrado told me, from traditions or writings kept in his family, ours were originally from Bergamo, then came into Carnia, where they had castles, then fell badly and scattered. But there are still some today at Mione and Muina in Carnia. We have arms: in the upper part of the shield a Greek cross crossed by two arrows, in the lower a pomegranate; above the shield a plumed helm.
carlo.why: Parenzo, 10 November 1876, to Giovanni Kobler. Every clause of it can now be checked against stone. The house at Gologorica carries ANNO DOMNI 1711 and this archive photographed it this week. The arms he describes from memory — cross, two arrows, pomegranate, plumed helm — are exactly what is carved on the cartouche above that inscription, on both tablets of his tomb, and on the urn beside it. And he names two villages: Mione and Muina. The family drove up the Val Degano this autumn and walked the graveyards of both.

rows.lab: Second, the Istarska Enciklopedija, which names the castle
rows.text: Miroslav Bertoša's entry for the surname: «predci gologoričkih rodova potječu iz Karnije, od tzv. gismanija, ministerijala akvilejskoga patrijarha» — the ancestors of the Gologorica line come from Carnia, of the so-called gismani, ministerials of the patriarch of Aquileia. The same word Carlo used. Then: «I De Franceschi possedevano il castello Agrons vicino al fiume Degano.» The De Franceschi possessed the castle of Agrons by the river Degano. — On which see the correction further down this page: the castle was rubble by 1400 and belonged to a different family, and what the Francisci held at Agrons was a ministerial fief. Charters of 1467 and 1471 record the investiture of a Leonardus Francisci by the governor of Friuli; a document of 1502 names «ser Leonardus Christoforus Francisci quondam Johannis gismanus de Carnia»; and the archives of the first half of the sixteenth century mention a de Franciscus «nel villaggio di Mione, sopra di Ovaro, nelle vicinanze del castello di Agrons» — in the village of Mione, above Ovaro, near the castle of Agrons.

rows.lab: Third, Brhan, who states it flatly and draws the line the archive most needed
rows.text: «I De Franceschi di Moncalvo erano originari di Agrons e i loro consanguinei abitavano nelle villa di Mione. Non sono da confondere con i numerosi De Franceschi carnici presenti in Istria in altre località o con i De Franceschi di Umago che hanno un origine completamente diversa.» The De Franceschi of Moncalvo were originally from Agrons and their kinsmen lived in the village of Mione. They are not to be confused with the many Carnian De Franceschi present in Istria in other places, or with the De Franceschi of Umago, who have a completely different origin. That last clause is the one this archive has been circling for weeks, and a scholar of the migration says it without being asked.

rows.lab: And the family had already been there
rows.text: Agrons is one of the four places the family photographed this autumn — Ovaro, Mione, Muina, Agrons — and its cemetery is in the files. The provincial interpretation panel at Santa Maria di Gorto, transcribed on this page above, describes the castle without knowing whose it was: «The Agrons Castle was close to the parish church of St. Mary; what remains visible nowadays is the bell tower only… During the Middle Ages, documents mention noblemen who were the feudal lords of the castle: Varnero and Vecello di Agrons in 1274, Pantaleone di Agrons in 1329. By 1400, the castle was already reduced to rubble and its stones were used to renovate the ancient church.» So the castle was already rubble when Leonardus Francisci was invested in 1467, and its stones are in the walls of the church this family's graves surround.

rows.lab: The line, as it now stands
rows.text: Agrons, by the Degano, where they held a castle already ruined by 1400 and were invested in 1467 and 1471 — Mione, above Ovaro, in the first half of the sixteenth century — and Moncalvo di Pisino, where the surname first appears in the baptismal register in 1661 and where Gian Battista, «il vecchio stipite del ramo dei De Franceschi», died in November 1686. Then the house of 1711. Three villages and two hundred and fifty years, and the first two are twenty minutes' walk apart.

rows.lab: Why the name splits three ways
rows.text: Carlo, in the same letter, explains it: «Il nostro nome originario è veramente De Franceschi… Ma venuti negli stati austriaci sembrò alle autorità che volessero arrogarsi il titolo di nobiltà, non sapendo questi che il de in Italia aggiunto al nome esprime il casato, e non titolo nobiliare, onde essi nei decreti scrivevano Defranceschi, e così avvenne che taluni per timore della multa comminata a chi s'arrogava… titolo di nobiltà, s'indussero a firmarsi Defranceschi, altri adottarono il De Franceschi, qualcuno perfino Franceschi.» Our original name is truly De Franceschi. But once in the Austrian lands the authorities took the «de» for a claim of nobility, not knowing that in Italy it means the house and not a title; so they wrote Defranceschi in their decrees, and some, fearing the fine laid on anyone who claimed nobility he could not prove, brought themselves to sign Defranceschi, others took De Franceschi, and a few even Franceschi. This site's title carries a fourth form, Defranceski, and the reason is the same clerk in a different century.

rows.lab: And one shoemaker, by name, going the other way
rows.text: Brhan's appendix transcribes the register of emigrants kept at Mione: «De Franceschi Matteo di Antonio e Maria, “Gracutta”, nato il 10 agosto 1756, calzolaio. Morto da qualche anno nell'Istria.» Matteo De Franceschi, son of Antonio and Maria, byname Gracutta, born 10 August 1756, shoemaker. Died some years ago in Istria. One man of this name, from this village, with a birth date, walking the road this page is about.

agrons.careful: What is and is not established. That the family of Gologorica came from Carnia is now stated by Carlo himself in 1876, by the Istarska Enciklopedija in 2005 and by Brhan, and it is not seriously in doubt. That they came specifically from Agrons and Mione rests on Bertoša and Brhan, who both cite Friulian charters this archive has not seen — the investitures of 1467 and 1471 and the document of 1502. Those are the papers to get, and they are in Udine. The Bergamo before Carnia is Carlo repeating what a cousin told him from family tradition, and this archive publishes it as exactly that. And the «gismani» are worth their own reading: the ministerials of the patriarch of Aquileia, a service nobility, which is a quite specific thing to claim.
agrons.source_agrons: Carlo De Franceschi to Giovanni Kobler, Parenzo, 10 November 1876, in «Lettere di Carlo De Franceschi a Giovanni Kobler», Fiume, rivista semestrale della Società di Studi Fiumani VI (1928), pp. 158–159 — held in this project's source library. Miroslav Bertoša, «De Franceschi», Istarska enciklopedija (2005), from istrianet.org. Dean Brhan, «L'emigrazione dalla Carnia verso l'Istria», in the Atti of Rovigno and in the extended version on istrianet.org. The Agrons castle history is from the provincial panel at Santa Maria di Gorto, photographed by the family, autumn 2026.
agrons.join: And the join with the section below is now obvious, though this archive published both halves without seeing it. The headmen's return of 1679, which Ferigo prints in full, lists the weavers gone into the County of Pazin village by village: from «Agrons e Cella» the Ruvis, and from «Mione» — «Zuane De Franceschi con un suo fiolo». Agrons is where the family held the castle in the fifteenth century. Mione is where the archives put them in the sixteenth. And in 1679 a Zuane De Franceschi of Mione is on the road to the imperial county with his son. Two villages a mile apart in one parish, two hundred years apart in the documents, and the same road out of both.

encyclopedia.heading: What the family did once it was there, from the Istrian encyclopedia
encyclopedia.lead: Bertoša's entry, written out of Camillo De Franceschi's own researches, gives the Gologorica family a shape this archive had only in pieces. It also settles an argument published on this site this morning.

rows.lab: 1661 — and the first man has a name and a trade
rows.text: «La prima menzione del cognome (mistro Zuanne de Franceschi) è del 1661.» The first mention of the surname — master Zuanne de Franceschi — is of 1661. Not just a year in a register: a name, and «mistro», the title of a master craftsman. The Croatian text has «mistro» and the Italian «ministro», and mistro is plainly the right reading for a man in a village of weavers. Zuanne is Venetian for Giovanni. Eighteen years later, in 1679, a Zuane De Franceschi of Mione is entered on the headmen's list of weavers gone into that same county.

rows.lab: November 1686 — the old stock dies
rows.text: «In novembre del 1686 muore a Montecalvo Gian Battista, che nel documento dell'archivio parrocchiale viene nominato il vecchio stipite del ramo dei De Franceschi.» In November 1686 Gian Battista died at Moncalvo, called in the parish document the old stock of the De Franceschi branch. Twenty-five years after the surname first appears there, the parish priest is already calling one of them the founder of the line.

rows.lab: 1712 — a De Franceschi in the castle prison at Pazin
rows.text: «Le fonti del 1712 menzionano Gian Battista, il parrocco a Montecalvo di Pisino, che ha preso le difese dei contadini nella rivolta contro le imposte del luogotenente del feudatario, per la quale ragione è stato arrestato e rinchiuso nel castello di Pisino, finché non lo ha liberato il signore di Montecalvo, il marchese de Prié.» Gian Battista, parish priest of Moncalvo, took the peasants' side in the revolt against the taxes of the fief-holder's lieutenant, and was arrested and shut in the castle of Pazin until the lord of Moncalvo, the Marquis de Prié, had him let out. A year after the house was built, a man of this name was in prison for defending the village against its landlord's agent — and was released by the landlord himself.

rows.lab: And a Belgian thread that keeps recurring
rows.text: The Marquis de Prié is a name from the Austrian Netherlands, and this site already records that Gologorica became in the eighteenth century the fief of Charles Antoine Biotz, «a Belgian from the diocese of Liège». Two Netherlandish lords of one Istrian village within a generation. That is not a coincidence but a fact about how Charles VI's court disposed of Istrian fiefs, and it is worth a page of its own.

rows.lab: What they were, in the eighteenth century
rows.text: Sebastian and his son Gian Battista, public notaries at Buzet and in Carnia. Francesco, doctor of medicine of Padua, practising at Montona, in other Istrian places, and in Carnia. Cosmo Damiano, surgeon, also of Padua. Filippo, son of Gian Battista, parish priest at Previs. Gian Matteo, son of Gian Pietro, parish priest at Moncalvo, canon of the cathedral of Pedena and apostolic protonotary. Note how many of them were still working in Carnia: the road stayed open in both directions for a century and a half after the crossing.

rows.lab: And it settles the Bribir argument
rows.text: This site published, this morning, a disagreement between Carlo and Kobler about who was castellan of Bribir. Carlo said his great-uncle Giovanni Battista, meant for the priesthood, took the sword instead, volunteered in Maria Theresa's army and was made castellan of Bribir. Kobler, from the Fiume registers, had a Giovanni son of Giovanni who died there in 1807. The encyclopedia gives: «Gian Battista II, figlio di secondo letto di Gian Battista, tenente, combatteva nella Guerra dei sette anni, e per i meriti ottenuti Maria Teresia gli ha affidato il controllo della difesa del castello di Bribir (1752–71).» A lieutenant in the Seven Years' War, given charge of the defence of Bribir by Maria Theresa, 1752 to 1771. That is Carlo's man, with dates, and a son of Gian Battista's second marriage. Kobler's Giovanni who died at Bribir in 1807 is a different and later man of the Fiume stock. Both were right and they were talking about two people.

encyclopedia.uspomene: One more thing off the same page, and it is an acquisition target. The entry's bibliography lists «Carlo De Franceschi, Uspomene, Pula i Rijeka 1989» — a Croatian translation of the «Memorie autobiografiche», published in 1989. This archive obtained the Italian original this morning from Trieste. A Croatian edition of it, made by Istrian scholars fifty years after the fact, will carry an apparatus the 1926 edition does not.
encyclopedia.source_enc: Miroslav Bertoša, «De Franceschi», in «Istarska enciklopedija», Leksikografski zavod Miroslav Krleža, Zagreb 2005, in Italian and Croatian in parallel, from istrianet.org. Its stated bibliography: Camillo De Franceschi, «Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino», AMSI 1963, vols 10–12; C. Pagnini, «In morte di Carlo De Franceschi», AMSI 1972–73; M. Bertoša, «Etos i etnos zavičaja», Pula and Rijeka 1985; Carlo De Franceschi, «Uspomene», Pula and Rijeka 1989. The charters of 1467, 1471 and 1502 are attributed by Bertoša to Camillo's own research, and are being traced.

gismani.heading: The gismani — what the family actually was in Carnia, and a correction
gismani.lead: The three charters have been traced. They cannot be read online and probably cannot be read anywhere except one private house and one box in Trieste. But tracing them turned up the Friulian scholarship on what these people were, and it is more specific — and less romantic — than «they had castles».

rows.lab: A gismano is not a nobleman with a castle. It is a member of a corporation
rows.text: The gismani were the ministerials of the Patriarch of Aquileia in Carnia, and they formed a recognised body — the third universitas of Carnia, standing beside the Quartieri and the town of Tolmezzo. They held their goods «jure recti et legalis feudi», by right of true and lawful fief; they were justiciable only before the Luogotenente's tribunal and not by the local courts; and they are described in the sources as «possessori delli beni di Gismania obbligati al servizio Militare». Patriarch Giovanni di Moravia's privilege of 9 August 1392 exempted them from watches, from guarding the passes and from the infantry levy — but not from the mounted militia owed to the Church of Aquileia. So the «obligation of military service» in the charters of 1467 and 1471 is the taglia di un cavallo armato, the tax of one armed horse.

rows.lab: Which makes those charters routine, and that is useful
rows.text: The Gorto gismani sought confirmation of their investitures collectively and repeatedly — in 1511 they appointed a procurator expressly «per ottenere conferma delle proprie investiture», and in 1525 they were still litigating the horse-tax. Charters of 1467 and 1471 four years apart are almost certainly two confirmations in that long series rather than two grants of a lordship. That is a smaller thing than it first sounded and a much more findable one.

rows.lab: And the correction, which matters
rows.text: This page said, a few hours ago, that the family «held a castle at Agrons». That overstates it and this archive should not have written it that way. The castle of Agrons was rubble by 1400 and belonged to a line called di Agrons — Werniero and Wecellio, sons of Giovanni da Agrons, in 1274. The Francisci appear at Agrons only from the fifteenth century, as gismani living in a village whose castle had already gone, and their surname comes from a man called Francesco, not from the place. There is no evidence connecting them to the di Agrons lords, and any descent from them should be treated as unsupported. What the family held at Agrons was a ministerial fief, which is a real and documented thing, and enough.

rows.lab: Friulian scholarship names them, without ever having heard of Gologorica
rows.text: Gabriele Siciliani's chapter «Jure recti et legalis feudi: la Carnia, Agrons e i gismani», in «Agrons. Storia di una comunità carnica dal Medio Evo all'Età Austriaca» (Società Filologica Friulana, Udine 2015), lists the gismanial families of the Canale di Gorto, and «de' Franceschi di Mione e Agrons» is among them. That is independent confirmation of Bertoša's claim from the Friulian end, in a book written by people with no interest in Istria at all.

printed.heading: And there are printed acts of the family, older than the charters
printed.lead: The same 2015 volume prints 273 documents of Agrons between 1270 and 1843, with regests and archival references. It does not contain the 1467, 1471 or 1502 charters. It contains these, which are in some ways better.

rows.lab: 6 August 1457, at Luincis
rows.text: «Pietro di Antonio Raineri da Agrons vende … a Leonardo del fu Francesco da Agrons, agente a nome del figlio Nicolò…» Peter, son of Antonio Raineri of Agrons, sells to Leonardo, son of the late Francesco, of Agrons, acting in the name of his son Nicolò. That is Leonardus quondam Francisci de Agrons — the man of the 1467 charter — ten years earlier, buying a rent-charge and already acting for a son.

Cristoforo, called Pizul, and Nicolò, sons of the late Giacomo di Francesco da Mione, resident at Agrons, sell a rent charged on their share of the tithe of Mione. A share of a tithe is a feudal right, and it is held by men described as of Mione and living at Agrons.

The testament of Gregorio, son of the late Leonardo Francisci of Mione, resident at Agrons, asking to be buried in the Pieve di Gorto «nella tomba dei suoi antenati» — in the tomb of his ancestors. The family drove to that church this autumn and photographed the graveyard around it.
Pietro, son of the late Leonardo De Franceschi of Mione. By now the surname is written the way Carlo would insist in 1876 was the original form.

rows.lab: And where the name itself may come from
rows.text: Giovanni Gortani, «Le vecchie famiglie di Gorto» (Tolmezzo 1898): «Nel 1443 Francesco q. Tomaso, o Timeo, d'Ovasta era passato a Mione» — in 1443 Francesco, son of the late Tomaso or Timeo, of Ovasta, had moved to Mione. A man called Francesco arriving at Mione in 1443, and by 1457 a Leonardo «del fu Francesco». A patronymic hardening into a surname, in one generation, in one village. This archive marks it as inference: it is the right shape and the right dates, and it is not proved. Gortani also has «un de Franceschi vivente nel 1421» at Luint.

gismani.where: So the three charters sit at the end of a chain that runs: Bertoša 2005, citing Camillo De Franceschi, who never published a line on Carnia or on his own family. The citation is therefore in Camillo's working papers, and the Trieste inventory says where. Cartolare 30, «Genealogia e storia», holds his «Regesti di pergamene carniche dell'archivio Magrini di Luint» — his own summaries of Carnian parchments in a private house at Luint, the hamlet next to Mione and Agrons — together with his research correspondence of 1889–1901, his son Carlo's correspondence with Udine and Venice in 1935–37, copies of the Gorto parish acts, and a dossier of «documenti comprovanti il possesso dello stemma, i diritti feudali e la civiltà della famiglia de Franceschi di Moncalvo», 1935–36. Proving feudal rights is exactly what a fifteenth-century investiture is for. On the evidence, the words Bertoša was paraphrasing are Camillo's regests, and the surviving copy of them is in one box at via Crispi 5 in Trieste.
gismani.negatives: Two negatives worth recording. The archive of the Luogotenente della Patria del Friuli is not at Udine at all — the «Guida generale degli Archivi di Stato» says plainly that «l'archivio del Luogotenente è nell'AS Venezia» — so the obvious hypothesis was wrong and is abandoned. And Camillo's «Storia documentata della Contea di Pisino», AMSI vols 62–64, 1962–64, pp. 7–490, is not digitised anywhere, so whether he printed these documents there could not be checked. Only the pre-1918 volumes of the Atti are online.
gismani.source_gismani: Giuliana Lucchini and Paolo Roseano (eds.), «Agrons. Storia di una comunità carnica dal Medio Evo all'Età Austriaca», Società Filologica Friulana, Udine 2015, 629 pp. — especially Gabriele Siciliani's chapter on the gismani and the 273 documents of its second part. Giovanni Gortani, «Le vecchie famiglie di Gorto», Tolmezzo 1898. Gilberto Dell'Oste, «Carte del vicariato foraneo di Gorto in Carnia (1270–1497)», Tolmezzo 1999. Mauro Bacci, «I Ministeriali del Patriarcato di Aquileia», Padua 2003. The inventory of the Archivio Camillo De Franceschi e famiglia, SIASP Trieste. None of these is yet held by this project; all are in print and obtainable.

svetvincenat.heading: Svetvinčenat — a third Carnian household of the name, and this archive had never looked
svetvincenat.lead: This page has followed the family from Agrons to Mione to Moncalvo. There was a third place, forty kilometres south, and four separate scholars have written about it while this archive was looking elsewhere. It came up because a search of the record indexes was rebuilt after being caught out, and Svetvinčenat came back second only to Rijeka.

rows.lab: 1734 — the household book of Svetvinčenat
rows.text: Danijela Doblanović, working the parish registers, isolates the surnames that appear in the «Status animarum» of 1734 in the town of Svetvinčenat itself and not in the surrounding villages: «Većinom je riječ o stanovnicima koji su došli s prostora Karnije… (prezimena De Franceschi, Crosila, Bergamo, Moro, Fiorencis i tako dalje)» — mostly inhabitants who came from the area of Carnia; the surnames De Franceschi, Crosila, Bergamo, Moro, Fiorencis and so on. And she adds what they did: «Krnjeli/Karnjeli su se uglavnom bavili trgovinom» — the Carnians were mainly engaged in trade.

rows.lab: And a second historian says the same
rows.text: Angelo Ciuffardi, on eighteenth-century Svetvinčenat: about three hundred and thirty inhabitants, «većinom venetskog ili karnijskog podrijetla» — mostly of Venetian or Carnian origin — and his list from the notarial records runs «Monti, Galante, Comin, Vorano, Volpi, Marani, Vernier, Manzin, Fiorencis, Zanetin, Lupieri, Defranceschi, Fabris, Bortolini, Manzoni, Bergamo, Zuliani». Lupieri and Fiorencis are Val di Gorto surnames. It is the same cohort, named twice by different scholars from different sources.

rows.lab: 1820 — and they were burghers, not peasants
rows.text: The house-owner protocol of the Franciscan cadastre for Svetvinčenat, transcribed by Altić and Kliman Grabar, gives three of the town's seventy-three houses to this surname: «Antonio de Franceschi (14/4)», «Pietro Antonio de Franceschi (29/51)» and «casa Antonio de Franceschi (30)». The authors note that «casa» marks the more important houses of the more prominent families. And the status column: only Grimani is a Ritter, a nobleman; a named group including de Franceschi is marked «Burgeri», citizens; and the majority are «Bauer», peasants.

rows.lab: Which is what Kandler and Brhan already said
rows.text: Pietro Kandler's mid-nineteenth-century list of the Carnian-origin families of Sanvincenti, printed by Brhan, has «Lupieri, Fiorencis, Defranceschi, Fabris, Vernier, Gonano, Vorano, Zuliani, Crosilla, Sandri, Corva, Spinotti e altre». And Brhan's own eighteenth-century notarial material gives «D.no Vittorio De Franceschi» among the landed proprietors, and a «Gasparo De Franceschi, carnico pure lui» — himself a Carnian — whose widow Maria Zanco left his capital, should their children die, to his kinswomen Pasqua and Antonia De Franceschi.

rows.lab: So: not one Carnian settlement in Istria, but at least three
rows.text: Gologorica in the Habsburg county of Pazin, where a Gian Battista is «il vecchio stipite» dead in November 1686 and where his descendant cut ANNO · DOMNI · 1711 over the door. Gračišće — Gallignana — the next parish east, where the same stock is in the baptism book by 1679 and where the direct line of this archive is still holding houses 5 and 19 into the nineteenth century: Joannes Baptista the farmer born 1787, Antonius the «lapidarius» born 1825, Josephus born 1863. And Svetvinčenat, over the border in Venetian Istria — a different state, a different landlord, a different set of parish books — with a household of the name established by 1734 and still holding three houses in 1820. Gologorica and Gračišće are four kilometres apart and share their people; Svetvinčenat is forty kilometres south and shares only the valley it came from. Whether that is one family arriving twice or two households out of the same Carnian valleys taking different roads is not answerable from anything this archive holds. What can be said is that the second one was there, that it was Carnian, that it traded rather than farmed, and that it ranked as citizens in a village of peasants.

rows.lab: And by 1945 it was one household
rows.text: The Yugoslav cadastre of 1945 counts a single «De Franceschi» family at Svetvinčenat. The «Stanza De Franceschi» farmstead that Brhan names among the holdings around the castle is gone from the map: the surviving stancija names are Grimani's and Stancovich's. Two hundred years, three houses, and then one.

rows.lab: And then the name kept going
rows.text: None of these three places is where the family is now. From Gračišće the direct line went down to Crikvenica on the Kvarner coast, and from there — by way of a labour camp at Pfullingen and a displaced-persons office — to Zimbabwe and to South Africa and to Australia. The wider surname went further and earlier: the largest cluster of all is in Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil from the 1880s, with names at Arroio do Tigre, Candelária and Porto Alegre; there is a thinner Argentine one from the same decade; the United States indexes carry forty-nine graves and a hundred and twenty-seven vital records, among them Basilio and Dario Defranceschi «born 26 September 1937 in GALLIGNANA, Austria» — the only American entry so far that names Gračišće outright. Australia holds fifteen graves and begins in 1949, with the post-war displacements. Which is the ordinary shape of it: a mountain valley empties into a province, the province empties into a coast, and the coast empties into four continents inside three generations.
rows.linktext: The country-by-country reckoning is on the Diaspora page

rows.lab: And they had a farmstead named after them
